name: Ustad Rahimuddin — Master Banarasi Silk Weaver
excerpt: Seven generations of Rahimuddin's family have woven silk in Varanasi's Madanpura. He is the last who knows kimkhab — a brocade so dense with gold it stands alone.
body:
Ustad Rahimuddin speaks of his loom the way others speak of a person. He has given it a name — Raushan, meaning light — because it has been in his family for four generations.

The loom is a Jacquard-type handloom, but do not call it simple. On it, Rahimuddin produces kimkhab — the most laborious form of Banarasi brocade, where gold and silver zari thread forms the base of the fabric, with silk used only as accent. A single sari can take eight months.

"I wake at 4 AM," he says, seated cross-legged before the loom in the half-light of his courtyard. "I work until Zuhr prayer. Then again from Asr until Isha. This is the life of a weaver."

His son works in software. His nephew drives an auto-rickshaw. The craft, if it survives, will survive through a niece who has shown interest. "She understands patience," Rahimuddin says. "Weaving is 90 percent patience and 10 percent prayer."

name: Ganga Devi — Brassware Maker
excerpt: Dhokra is the oldest known metal-casting tradition in the world — four thousand years old, using the lost-wax process. Ganga Devi makes ritual objects for the ghats in the same way her ancestors made them.
body:
Dhokra casting uses the lost-wax method: a wax form is made, coated in clay, fired until the wax melts out (leaving a hollow mold), and then filled with molten brass. When the clay is broken, a unique metal object remains. Every piece is therefore different — it cannot be exactly replicated.

Ganga Devi's workshop is small, dark, and filled with the smell of burning beeswax. She makes diyas (oil lamps), incense holders, and small deity figurines — the objects needed for the daily rituals of the ghats.

"The priests need these every season," she says, shaping a thin wax rope into the edge of a diya. "New ones when old ones wear out. I have made the same diya hundreds of times, but never twice the same."

Her family's brass-casting tradition predates any written record in Varanasi. She cannot trace it back further than her great-grandmother. But the process itself — the wax, the clay, the fire — has not changed.
